title: Tempranillo
description: Also called Tinta Roriz and Aragonez in Portugal, Tinto Fino in Ribera. Spain's great red, shaped by oak and time.
L: Tempranillo gives medium to full-bodied wines with red cherry, strawberry, plum and dried fig, plus tobacco, leather and earth with age. Tannin is medium to high, acidity medium. Its fruit is fairly neutral, so oak and ageing shape it a lot. It's the third or fourth most planted red grape in the world.

Tempranillo comes from temprano, Spanish for early, because it ripens earlier than other Spanish grapes. DNA shows it's a cross of Albillo Mayor and Benedicto, probably from the Ebro valley. It has thick skins, giving deep colour, but naturally modest acidity, so it suits places with cool nights.
What does Tempranillo's name refer to?

Young Tempranillo is ruby, with red fruit and soft tannin. Aged Rioja is paler, garnet, with dried fruit, leather, and vanilla, coconut or dill from American oak. Ribera del Duero is darker and more powerful. The combination of red fruit with leather and oak is a classic clue.
Red fruit plus leather and oak
Tempranillo has naturally very high acidity.
Not true. Its acidity is medium to modest, which is why cool nights or high sites help.
Tempranillo gives red fruit, leather and tobacco
Its name means early; it's a cross from the Ebro valley
Oak and ageing shape its style

Tempranillo grows across Spain: Rioja, Ribera del Duero, Toro, Navarra, La Mancha, Valdepeñas. Each has a local name: Tinto Fino or Tinta del País in Ribera, Tinta de Toro in Toro, Cencibel in La Mancha, Ull de Llebre in Catalonia. In Portugal it's Tinta Roriz in the Douro and Aragonez in the Alentejo.

Tempranillo needs warmth to ripen but cool nights to keep acidity. That's why it thrives on high plateaus, like Ribera del Duero at 750 to 1,000 m, and in Rioja Alta with Atlantic influence. In very hot places it can lose acidity and turn flat. It's also grown in Argentina, Australia and the US.
Match each name to its region.
Tempranillo changes names as it crosses Iberia.

Tempranillo's thick skins give good colour and resistance to rot, but make it sensitive to drought and pests. Its early ripening suits continental climates with short seasons. Higher, cooler sites have become popular as summers grow warmer.
Why do high plateaus suit Tempranillo?
Cool nights keep its modest acidity
Cool nights balance warm days and preserve freshness.
Tempranillo grows across Spain and Portugal under many names
It needs warm days and cool nights
High plateaus like Ribera suit it well
Describe Tempranillo in Ribera del Duero

Rioja, along the Ebro, is Tempranillo's most famous home. It's usually blended with Garnacha, Graciano and Mazuelo. Rioja Alta and Rioja Alavesa, higher and cooler, give elegant, structured wines; Rioja Oriental, warmer, gives riper ones. Traditional Rioja ages long in American oak, giving vanilla, coconut and dill.

Ribera del Duero, on the high Meseta, makes mostly single-variety Tinto Fino. Vineyards at 750 to 1,000 m have hot days and very cold nights. The wines are darker, fuller and more powerful than Rioja, often aged in French oak. Vega Sicilia, since 1864, and Pingus are famous names.
How does Ribera del Duero Tempranillo typically compare with Rioja?
High altitude and big diurnal range give Ribera its depth and power.

Rioja is traditionally a blend, more about elegance and oak-aged complexity. Ribera is usually pure Tempranillo, more about fruit concentration and power. Both have modern producers using French oak and shorter ageing, and traditionalists using long ageing. Toro, further west, is even riper and more muscular.
Which grapes are often blended with Tempranillo in Rioja?
Rioja blends Tempranillo and often ages it in American oak
Ribera del Duero makes powerful, pure Tinto Fino at altitude
Rioja leans to elegance; Ribera and Toro to power

Spain's law sets minimum ageing for reds. Crianza: 24 months, at least 6 in oak. Reserva: 36 months, at least 12 in oak. Gran Reserva: 60 months, at least 18 in oak. Joven, young, has little or no oak. These terms appear on the back label, often with a seal.

Rioja sets stricter oak rules. Crianza needs at least 12 months in barrel. Reserva needs 12 months in barrel and 36 months in total. Gran Reserva needs 24 months in barrel and 60 months in total. Tempranillo's thick skins and moderate tannins suit long oak ageing, which softens it and adds vanilla, spice and leather.
Order the Rioja categories by minimum ageing.
Each step demands more time in barrel and bottle.

Long ageing changes Tempranillo: fruit shifts from fresh red cherry to dried fig and prune, colour fades from ruby to garnet and brick, and tertiary notes of leather, tobacco, mushroom and cedar appear. Traditional Gran Reservas, from producers like López de Heredia, can be drunk 30 years later.
From fresh fruit to leather and tobacco
How long must a Rioja Gran Reserva spend in barrel at minimum?
24 months in barrel, within 60 months of total ageing.
Spain's law sets Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva ageing
Rioja requires longer barrel ageing than the national minimum
Ageing turns Tempranillo's fruit into leather and tobacco
Describe Tinta Roriz in the Douro
Explain its role in Portuguese blends

In the Douro, Tempranillo is called Tinta Roriz. It's one of the five recommended grapes for Port, with Touriga Nacional and Touriga Franca. In dry Douro reds, it adds red fruit, body and fine tannins to blends. It's one of the most planted grapes in the region.
Tinta Roriz: Port and dry reds

In the hot Alentejo, Tempranillo is called Aragonez. It's often blended with Trincadeira and Alicante Bouschet, giving ripe, soft, fruity reds. The heat can make it lose acidity, so cooler sites near the São Mamede mountains are valued. Aragonez is among the region's most planted reds.
Match each name to its Portuguese role.
In Portugal, Tempranillo plays a supporting role in blends.
Portugal's Dão also grows Tinta Roriz, in elegant blends with Touriga Nacional and Jaen.
In Portugal, Tempranillo is mostly made as a single-variety wine.
Not true. It's mainly a blending partner, with Touriga Nacional in the Douro or Trincadeira in the Alentejo.
Tinta Roriz is a key Douro grape, for Port and dry reds
In Portugal it's usually a blending partner

Tempranillo suits roast lamb, especially Castilian lechazo, suckling lamb, a classic with Ribera. Rioja goes with grilled lamb chops over vine cuttings, chorizo, jamón ibérico and Manchego cheese. Aged Gran Reserva suits mushrooms and game. Joven suits tapas.

Serve at 16 to 18 degrees. Joven within two years; Crianza within five; Reserva five to fifteen; Gran Reserva 15 to 30 years or more. Old Rioja can throw sediment; decant gently. Ribera's big young wines benefit from air.
Which Castilian dish is a classic with Ribera del Duero?
Roast suckling lamb in wood ovens is Ribera's traditional match.
A Rioja Reserva with jamón ibérico is a simple, classic Spanish pairing. The ham's fat and salt soften the wine's tannin.
Sorbet is too sweet and acidic for a red.
Tempranillo suits lamb, jamón and Manchego
Gran Reservas age 15 to 30 years or more

American oak's lactones give coconut and vanilla.
